title: Hypergraph cut sparsifiers with \(O(n/\varepsilon ^{2})\) hyperedges
formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge 2\), every nonnegatively weighted hypergraph H on \(V=[n]\), and every real \(\varepsilon \in (0,1/2)\), there is a nonnegatively weighted hypergraph \(H'\) on the same V with at most \(Cn/\varepsilon ^{2}\) hyperedges and \((1- \varepsilon )\operatorname{cut}_{H}(S)\le \operatorname{cut}_{H}' (S)\le (1+\varepsilon )\operatorname{cut}_{H}(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq V\) simultaneously?
why: Tests whether preserving all cuts of a multiway interaction system requires any more hyperedges than the graph sparsification upper bound. It separates the number of retained interactions from their incidence storage and from the cost of computing them.
status_note: Checked through 11 September 2026. No \(Cn/\varepsilon ^{2}\) existence theorem or matching refutation was located. The old quadratic upper bound has been superseded by \(O(n \log  n/\varepsilon ^{2})\). The original source permits an arbitrary weighted hypergraph on the same vertices; this card preserves that scope. Later near-optimal storage statements do not remove the logarithmic edge-count gap.

progress.text: Batson–Spielman–Srivastava achieve the graph edge-count benchmark through spectral sparsification.
Krauthgamer poses the \(O(n/\varepsilon ^{2})\) same-vertex hypergraph existence question.
Chen–Khanna–Nagda obtain \(O(n \log  n/\varepsilon ^{2})\) hyperedges, eliminating the prior rank dependence.
Near-optimal sketching addresses bit complexity, with logarithmic factors retained.
Insertion-only streaming space improves without proving the exact edge-count target.

sentences: A hypergraph cut counts the total weight of hyperedges meeting both sides of a vertex partition.
A cut sparsifier replaces the hypergraph by a smaller weighted hypergraph that approximately preserves every cut at once.
The question asks whether O(n/epsilon squared) hyperedges always suffice for multiplicative error epsilon.
This matches the natural target from ordinary graphs, while a hyperedge can involve arbitrarily many vertices.
The size measure counts hyperedges rather than their total incidence size, making the project specifically about how many distinct multiway interactions must be retained.

definitions: A hypergraph \(H=(V,E,w)\) has \(E\subseteq \{e\subseteq V:|e|\ge 2\}\) and weights \(w:E\to \mathbb{R} _{\ge 0}\). Its cut value is \(\operatorname{cut}_{H}(S)=\Sigma\)_{\(e\in E: e\cap S\ne \varnothing\) and \(e\cap (V\setminus S)\ne \varnothing\)}\(w(e): a\) crossing hyperedge contributes its weight once, independently of how many of its vertices lie on either side. Zero-weight edges may be discarded; repeated edges can be merged by summing weights. Empty or singleton hyperedges never cross a cut and are omitted without loss. \(H' =(V,E' ,w' )\) follows the same conventions, with arbitrary nonnegative real weights. The output edge set \(E'\) need not be a subset of E, following the original problem statement; new vertices are not permitted. Size means |\(E' |\), not \(\sum_{e\in E'}|e|\), weight-encoding length or total storage bits. C is independent of \(n, \varepsilon\), edge count, rank and all weights. The empty edge set is allowed, and a zero input cut must remain exactly zero. This is a finite-object existence question: no construction algorithm, running-time or probability guarantee is imposed.
answer_criterion: Prove the universal existence statement with one constant C, or prove that the minimum required number of hyperedges times \(\varepsilon ^{2}/n\) is unbounded over the permitted inputs and accuracies. For a negative answer, the lower bound must allow arbitrary nonnegative hyperedges on the original vertex set. A growing logarithmic factor or a counterexample only to a particular sampling method does not resolve the target.

context_blocks.text: A sparsifier replaces a large interaction structure by a smaller one while preserving the values needed for later cut computations. The guarantee holds for every partition at once, including a partition chosen after seeing the sparsifier. A separate approximation for one predetermined cut would be much weaker. A hypergraph can contain exponentially many distinct hyperedges on n vertices, so reducing their number to near linear can be a large compression.

The cut convention is important for multiway interactions. A hyperedge \(\{1,2,3,4\}\) of weight one contributes one to both the partition \(\{1\}|\{2,3,4\}\) and the partition \(\{1,2\}|\{3,4\}\). Replacing it by a uniformly weighted clique gives contributions proportional to three and four respectively. Thus the ordinary graph representation does not automatically preserve the hypergraph’s cut function.

The formulation follows the broad source question: the approximating hypergraph may introduce different hyperedges on the same vertices. Requiring only reweighting and deleting original edges is an additional restriction. A construction satisfying that stronger condition also answers the stated existence question, but a lower bound restricted to that condition would not by itself refute it.

Ordinary graphs already admit \(O(n/\varepsilon ^{2})\)-edge sparsifiers. Batson, Spielman and Srivastava prove a spectral guarantee, which implies the required cut inequalities by substituting zero-one indicator vectors. This gives the benchmark without a logarithmic overhead. For hypergraphs, preserving an associated energy on all real vectors is also stronger than preserving cut indicators, and the particular energy definition must be specified before importing a spectral result.

The quadratic-in-n bound quoted in the 2018 problem entry is outdated. Chen, Khanna and Nagda give a randomized polynomial-time construction using \(O(n \log  n/\varepsilon ^{2})\) reweighted original hyperedges. Their result removes the extra dependence on maximum hyperedge size. The remaining log n is unbounded, so it cannot be absorbed into the universal C in this card.

Subsequent sketching and streaming results address how a sparsifier can be represented or maintained with limited memory. A rank-r hyperedge can require r vertex identifiers, so near-linear hyperedge count does not mean near-linear bit storage independent of r. The FOCS 2024 sketch bounds retain logarithmic factors in their near-linear output guarantee.
The ICLR 2026 insertion-only work further improves memory use, but its guarantees also retain logarithmic factors. Its space theorem does not establish the \(Cn/\varepsilon ^{2}\) hyperedge count.

Resolving the target would determine whether hypergraph cuts admit the same upper bound on the number of interactions as graph cuts at each accuracy. It would not automatically remove the cost of describing large hyperedges or reading the original input. Those separate costs explain why stronger data-access and streaming results can coexist with an unresolved existence question.
